The disruption affected departing flights but did not impact aircraft already in the air or services operated by United Express, while FlightAware reported 418 delayed United flights late Monday afternoon.
United subsequently resolved the technical issue and apologized to affected passengers, adding that there was no indication the outage was related to a cybersecurity incident.

Reports of these issues began spiking at noon, with complaints to Downdetector rising from a dozen at 9 a.m. to more than 3,600 by 1 p.m., and more than 4,000 reports submitted by 1:30 p.m. ET.

Chase spokeswoman Stephanie Gostomski said some transactions are taking longer than usual but customers "still have access to their accounts and funds," while some customers received messages stating "Some services aren't available."

The outages follow a major Microsoft outage that began Friday, impacting Outlook and Teams, and occur just three days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop following a communications failure.
Many customers remain unable to cash checks or transfer funds at local branches, which The Dispatch witnessed, and Chase has not provided a timeline for when services will be fully restored.

Judge William Sullivan denied a defense motion to dismiss charges following a September mistrial, when jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict on any count. Sullivan did not question the holdout juror before declaring mistrial.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington argues Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis, noting she "was not very good" and remained "suicidal" at the time. Prosecutors maintain she planned the killings ahead of time.
Recent court rulings rejected defense requests to question the holdout juror and denied a prosecution bid to restrict media discussions. The final pretrial hearing is scheduled for March 18.

The case continues to draw online speculation surrounding her husband, Patrick Clancy. For those in crisis, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is available by calling 988 or texting HOME to 741741.
title: Lindsay Clancy will be retried next year in the deaths of her three children, judge says

Trump and Kim held three meetings during the president's first term, including summits in Singapore and Hanoi, after the U.S. leader initially mocked Kim as "rocket man" during a 2017 speech.

summary: On Monday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Trump's tariffs have disrupted Canada's auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production, prompting Canada to recently threaten legal action against Stellantis after shifting Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois.

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, allowing up to 49,000 imports annually, though Carney insists any new Chinese investment must involve substantial domestic manufacturing and labor standards.
Carney is in Cambodia for the Francotech Summit and will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing investment is expected to be discussed.

While negotiations with the United States remain his priority, Carney emphasized Monday that Canada is prepared to pursue alternatives involving European, Chinese, or Japanese automakers if a viable regional auto industry cannot be preserved.

The NSA instructed employees to arrive in staggered shifts throughout Tuesday morning, citing a "heightened security threat" as the agency works to understand the outage's scope.
Officials state there is no immediate evidence of a cyberattack, though the source of the technical failure remains unknown as the NSA assesses the disruption.

title: Highly classified US national security communications network is down, CNN reports

summary: On Tuesday, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell four points to 25, marking the lowest builder sentiment since April 2012 as mortgage rates and labor shortages weaken the housing market.

NAHB Chairman Bill Owens attributed the decline to stepped-up immigration enforcement keeping legal workers off job sites and higher fuel prices forcing subcontractors to raise rates sharply, causing builders to scale back construction.

With fewer buyers in the market, 46% of builders reduced prices this month, the highest post-Covid share, while 68% deployed sales incentives—the 20th consecutive month at least 60% of builders used them.

Prospective buyer traffic fell two points to 16, hitting a 15-year low, while current sales conditions declined six points to 28 and future expectations dropped two points to 30 across all HMI components.

Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, cited building material costs pushed higher by tariffs and excessive regulations as undermining affordability; mortgage rates above 7% and economic uncertainty continue holding buyers back.
title: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices

Dijkmans entered the United States on a tourist visa, which prohibits employment. Her mother, Marianne Scholt, acknowledged her daughter missed an immigration appointment for her Green Card application, likely flagging her within the ICE system.

Scholt reported that conditions inside Delaney Hall are 'very distressing,' citing limited food, poor hygiene, and phone access reduced to five minutes per call. Dijkmans shares quarters with 12 other detainees, with only four phones available for 60 people.

Dutch Embassy officials confirmed they are providing consular assistance, though privacy restrictions prevent commenting on specifics. Scholt visited her daughter on Saturday and reported she was 'in tears' and barely recognized in detention clothing.

The governor announced a "92 County Affordability Tour" to "meet directly with Hoosiers about the cost-of-living challenges facing their families" while discussing his economic agenda.

Braun faces a complex political landscape after Indiana Republicans lost their House supermajority in the November 3 midterm election, with potential primary challengers emerging within the state party.

The Indiana Democratic Party criticized Braun's record, alleging Hoosiers struggle with rising costs, as the general election approaches November 7, 2028. Braun aims to build on his affordability platform to secure a second term.
title: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun Announces 2028 Reelection Bid

summary: On Tuesday, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau reported U.S. retail sales rose 0.2% in October, a slowdown from the 0.8% gain in September as shoppers became cautious amid high prices.

Declining purchases of big-ticket items drove the cooling trend, with motor vehicle and parts dealers posting a 1.6% drop, furniture and home furnishings stores falling 2.3%, and clothing and accessories stores declining 0.7%.

Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at TransUnion, noted outstanding credit card balances hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from last year, supporting consumer spending despite economic headwinds.
Target is marketing more than 8,000 new gifts for the Thanksgiving weekend, with most items priced at $20 or less, as retailers prepare for the unofficial start of holiday shopping.

Credit card balances per active account are increasing at a 9% yearly pace, the fastest since before the pandemic, while households save less and dip into nest eggs to afford purchases, according to Brian LeBlanc, head of economic analysis at PNC Financial.
title: U.S. Retail Sales Rise 0.2% in October as Shoppers Turn Cautious

summary: On Tuesday, attorney Abbe Lowell signaled that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook will not attend a White House hearing investigating mortgage fraud allegations. The refusal extends Cook's dispute with the administration over her appearance before the committee.

The White House committee investigating allegations Cook committed mortgage fraud in 2021 comprises economic adviser Kevin Hassett, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission lead Andrea Lucas, and Labor Secretary pick Keith Sonderling. President Donald Trump has sought Cook's removal since August 2025.

Lowell stated in a letter that Cook has "no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing," citing a duty to protect the Federal Reserve's independence. He characterized the committee as "pretextual" and a threat to the institution.

Prior warnings from President Donald Trump's administration stated the committee "reserves the right to draw adverse inferences" against Cook if she fails to participate. The escalation intensifies the standoff over her potential removal.

In June, the Supreme Court blocked Trump from removing Cook, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve." The Court noted Trump could try again if he provided adequate notice.
title: Lawyer for Fed's Cook threatens to not take part in 'unfair' White House hearing

Schools implemented these restrictions to address a global decline in student achievement that began around 2013, aiming to minimize classroom distractions and recover lost instructional time.
The study found that lockable pouches—costing about $25 to $30 per student—reduced in-school phone activity by approximately 20 percent across the 4,600 campuses examined.

Although bans added the equivalent of one or two weeks of annual instruction, Stanford University economist Thomas Dee called early results "disappointing," noting students still use other devices like laptops.

Harvard professor Tom Kane, a study co-author, emphasized that while bans are cost-effective, they are not a "panacea," as researchers continue examining social media 's broader impact on student learning.
title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores

Evidence linking EDCs to health disorders "is strong and continues to grow" since 2012, yet more than 350,000 chemicals registered globally remain largely unevaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties.

While the American Chemistry Council argues existing frameworks like the Toxic Substances Control Act effectively manage risk, experts contend current policies remain "fragmented and insufficient." The industry contributed $1.65 million to support chemical management systems.

Bjorn Beeler of the International Pollutants Elimination Network described the projected surge in plastic production as a "toxic tidal wave" no one is prepared for, urging a shift toward proactive prevention.

Negotiations to address chemical pollution are set to resume early next year. Lead author Laura Vandenberg emphasized that reducing exposure requires action at a policy level throughout society rather than relying on individual consumer choices.
title: Latest science shows chemicals in many everyday items pose a growing threat, UN report says

summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced in Manila that Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports under a pending trade agreement expected to be finalized in the coming weeks.
Accounting for 24.6% of total exports, the US represents Thailand's largest market; the country initially faced a threatened 36% US tariff in 2025, which Washington lowered to 19%.

Under the agreement, Thailand will remove non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol, and poultry while committing to purchase an estimated $2.6 billion in additional US agricultural products.
Appearing with Trump at the signing, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul stated the agreement will bring "greater dynamics to our trade relations and open new opportunities for all stakeholders."

Trump began a three-day visit to the Philippines following the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, which includes the Quad group's first meeting in two years and the Asia -Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen.

Both foreground “Iran war ” and predict the nominee will “likely face” questions, making escalation the pivotal dividing line, though neither supplies substantive details.
Center coverage broadens the lens, uniquely identifying Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and portraying a potentially “fierce debate” over Iran, military transparency, and sailors’ well-being.
Across perspectives, Trump’s selection, the nominee’s scheduled Senate Armed Services Committee testimony, and the hearing’s procedural role remain shared ground.
summary: On Tuesday, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testifies before the Senate Armed Services Committee, the first step in a confirmation process requiring a congressional waiver due to his recent active-duty service.

To secure the permanent post, Cao must overcome a legal prohibition against military officers serving as service secretaries within seven years of retirement, a rare exception granted only three times since 1950.
Democrats are expected to scrutinize Cao over the Iran war , including major damage to the 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, and reports of crew stress on the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Lawmakers from both parties have historically expressed aversion to waiver precedents, citing concerns about eroding civilian control of the military, as Republicans currently control the chamber before Democrats take charge in January.
The hearing follows a failed impeachment attempt in the House against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, occurring amidst broader debates regarding transparency and the unpopular Iran war.
title: Trump Navy Nominee Faces Iran War Questions at Confirmation Hearing

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the poll as evidence of communal alienation and a “feeling of impunity” toward antisemitism , portraying Mélenchon as a “left-wing populist” whose victory could prompt emigration.

Right-Leaning coverage intensifies the warning, labeling him a “far-left leader,” stressing “rising levels of antisemitism,” and adding that 64% considered leaving, 82% experienced antisemitism, and 29% removed mezuzahs.

Center coverage mainly presents the conditional 69% figure and a “major shift” in perceived political “threats.” The dividing line is whether concern reflects broader insecurity or Mélenchon-specific danger; all emphasize Jewish vulnerability and emigration, reflecting wider ideological conflict over France’s left and antisemitism.
summary: A new survey released Sunday by the American Jewish Committee found that 64% of French Jews have considered leaving the country, up from 52% in 2024. The Ifop polling institute and Foundation for Political Innovation conducted the study.

Since the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre in Israel, deepening fears grip the Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism . According to findings, 82% of French Jews have experienced antisemitism, and 66% no longer believe France is a safe country.

The prospect of a Melenchon presidency provoked even greater concern, with 69% of respondents saying they might emigrate if the far-left leader wins the 2027 election. Among French Jews, 86% believe Jean-Luc Melenchon contributes to rising antisemitism.

Anne-Sophie Sebban-Bache, AJC vice president for Europe, told Ynet there is a "crisis of trust" between the Jewish community and the French Republic. Only 22% of victims report incidents to police, while 65% deem punishments for antisemitic offenses insufficiently severe.

Despite widespread recognition that antisemitism is increasing, only 38% of French respondents say they would demonstrate against it, down from 46% in 2024. Meanwhile, 49% of young French adults aged 18 to 24 compare Israel's treatment of Palestinians to Nazi Germany's persecution of Jews.
title: About 69% of French Jews would consider leaving France if Mélenchon elected, AJC-IFOP poll shows

bias: Left-Leaning coverage urges voters to “get rid of” Netanyahu, says he “burned every support” in Washington, links his alliance with Trump to Democratic gains, and anticipates renewed peace pressure.
Center coverage frames the partnership as a “lost bet,” stresses Israel’s “increasingly isolated” position, and warns Hamas could “win big” from turmoil.

Right-Leaning coverage instead says October 7 “shattered” Netanyahu’s “grip on power,” treats coalition losses as a stability crisis, and places him within a “global far-right alliance.” All portray Netanyahu and Trump as politically weakened, but diverge over whether the decisive issue is diplomacy, strategic fallout, or wartime accountability.
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lost his parliamentary majority following a heated vote, while President Donald Trump's party suffered a major midterm election setback.
President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to end $3.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid, with the president announcing the assistance would cease by the end of the year.
Vice President JD Vance acknowledged the war with the Islamic Republic of Iran contributed to Republican defeats, as voters rejected the administration's "incessant message to hate thy neighbor."

Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak accused Netanyahu of concocting a "stinking deal" that traded military aid for political endorsement, concluding Netanyahu "exceeded his authority" and is "utterly unfit to lead a country."

Political uncertainty in Israel and Washington may provide Hamas additional room to maneuver over its future governance role, as the militant movement continues to survive despite three years of full-scale war.
title: NETANYAHU LOSES PARLIAMENTARY MAJORITY AS TRUMP’S REPUBLICANS SUFFER MAJOR CONGRESSIONAL SETBACK!

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Huang’s possible return through the “scandal,” “abruptly” stepping down, reported affairs, and potential national-security risks, making controversy the pivotal test of leadership.

Right-Leaning coverage emphasizes his “mistake,” regret, employee and investor support, the board’s security committee, and a 2.5% share decline, portraying accountability and institutional stability as competing concerns.

Center coverage narrows the story to his conditional willingness, board approval, and an “outpouring of support.” Across perspectives, “breaks his silence” adds drama, while “honored” softens the prospect of return.
All agree the board holds the decision, reflecting broader tensions over scandal, governance, markets, and security.
summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang broke his silence on Tuesday, issuing a statement saying he would be "honored" to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company's best interest.

Huang resigned 33 years after co-founding the company following reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at a Singapore-based customer whom sources identified as a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

An online petition urging the board to reinstate Huang had about 180,000 signatures on Monday, though CNBC reported that directors are currently not considering his return and remain focused on their investigation.

Nvidia reports third-quarter results after the market closes on Tuesday, with analysts expecting earnings of $2.47 a share on revenue of $109.15 billion, as Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress leads the call.
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress on December 1, positioning the company to address ongoing geopolitical and national security concerns as it navigates leadership uncertainty.
title: Jensen Huang Breaks Silence, Signals Willingness to Return as Nvidia CEO

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Florida’s floating solar as “sustainable energy ,” emphasizing “scarce” and “costly” land, the scale of tens of thousands of retention ponds, and an innovative path to clean-power expansion; right-leaning coverage de-emphasizes that broader climate narrative, stressing instead that costs are falling and solar can grow without using additional land.

The left’s optimistic, solution-oriented tone contrasts with the right’s restrained, market-and-efficiency framing, though neither uses strongly partisan language such as “woke” or “crisis.” Center coverage bridges them with technical explanations of buoyant panels and anchors.
All agree the technology is becoming cheaper and more established, reflecting a wider divide over environmental aspiration versus practical economics.
summary: Florida is turning thousands of its retention ponds into solar energy sites, leveraging a 2022 state law that explicitly supports floating photovoltaics to meet growing electricity demand in the Sunshine State.

Falling costs drove adoption, with median project expenses dropping about 48% to $1.25 per watt since 2015; Florida's estimated 76,000 stormwater ponds provide ideal, otherwise unused locations within city limits.

Floating systems produce about 5% to 8% more power than rooftop arrays because of water's cooling effect, according to Justin Kramer, director of emerging technologies and data analytics at the Orlando Utilities Commission.

To protect local ecosystems, the Orlando Utilities Commission limits coverage to 70% to 80% of pond surfaces, as AJ Reisinger of the University of Florida cautioned that shading can alter aquatic photosynthesis and habitat.

Globally, floating solar accounts for less than 1% of capacity, with Asia leading development; scientist Oktoviano Gandhi noted lenders have gained confidence in the technology's reliability after about 20 years of deployment.
title: Florida’s stormwater ponds become floating solar farms as costs fall and demand rises

bias: Left-Leaning framing treats Democratic “big wins” as a force that could “reshape” immigration and abortion debates, giving the victories an expansive, consequential tone.

Right-Leaning coverage uses the same “big wins” wording but places greater emphasis on political shifts, divided government, and the bishops’ broader priorities, including artificial intelligence—implicitly underscoring constraints and possible concern.
Center-Leaning accounts intensify the result as “sweeping” and describe a “reset” in political dynamics.

All perspectives agree that bishops met in Baltimore after the midterms, while their differing emphasis reflects wider ideological divides over electoral power, policy influence, and church engagement.
summary: U.S. Catholic Bishops are holding their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week as the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops faces a divided government following Democrats' sweeping midterm victories.

Catholic voters split roughly evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House according to The AP Voter Poll, though White Catholics and Latino Catholics showed distinct voting patterns.

After the White House released images of bishops praying over Republican President Donald Trump in the Oval Office in late October, the Church's non-partisan message became muddled, prompting at least two bishops to express regret.

Bishops are expected to hear updates Wednesday from their committees on migration and abortion , while also launching a new task force focused on preserving human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.

Last fall, the Conference issued a "special message" decrying "the vilification of immigrants," positioning the Church to influence policy as bishops emphasize that elected officials must be devoted to pursuing what is right and just.
title: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats’ big wins help reshape immigration and abortion debates

bias: Left- and right-leaning coverage largely converge, framing the federal review through charged terms like “leadership failures,” “driving factors,” and “destroyed,” emphasizing institutional accountability rather than the fire as an unavoidable disaster.

The center perspective adds operational specificity—“not qualified to lead,” “ignored warning signs,” a week of monitoring amid extreme heat and dry winds—and stresses that no single person or cause explains the losses.
Thus, the pivotal divide is breadth versus qualification: left and right present a sweeping management indictment, while center details delegation, training, and communication breakdowns.
All emphasize the lodge’s destruction and preparedness failures, reflecting shared concern over governmental competence and disaster response.
summary: A federal report released recently identified systemic weaknesses in the National Park Service's response to the 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire at Grand Canyon National Park, noting foreseeable failures in preparedness and leadership hindered decision-making at critical moments.
Lightning sparked the blaze in 2025, but park leaders chose to monitor the fire for one week despite warnings about persistent drought and extreme heat, according to the Interior Department review.
The fire destroyed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge, cabins, and employee housing along the North Rim, resulting in suppression costs that topped $141 million over three months.

A breakdown in communication delayed fire retardant use until after critical structures were lost, the Interior Department report found, despite the National Park Service's initial defense citing extreme wind conditions.

Experts warned the 2025 incident serves as a critical case study, recommending that agency administrators undergo complex incident training and ensure communication flows through proper channels for future wildfire management.
title: Federal review faults leadership failures in Grand Canyon fire that destroyed lodge

bias: Left-Leaning coverage pairs Disney ’s “robust” or “stellar” quarter with scrutiny of the $3 billion savings plan and “layoffs,” while highlighting streaming, AI, and Marvel viewership.

Right-Leaning coverage frames the same results through “surges,” “boost,” parks, ESPN, content investment, and dividends, de-emphasizing job cuts and emphasizing shareholder gains; its pivotal dividing line is whether efficiency signals opportunity or workforce risk.
Center coverage bridges these narratives, noting growth alongside layoffs that “loom,” restructuring, and investor implications.

All perspectives emphasize the 16% revenue increase to $25.9 billion and earnings beating expectations, reflecting broader tensions between market optimism, labor concerns, and corporate transformation.
summary: On Tuesday, The Walt Disney Company reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $25.95 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.77 per share, beating Wall Street expectations across all three core divisions.
CEO Josh D'Amaro continues restructuring efforts, with management seeking 20% annual savings through job eliminations as the company aims to generate $3 billion in run-rate savings by fiscal 2029.
Streaming revenue climbed 19% to $6.1 billion and the Experiences division posted record revenue, supported by strong NFL viewership and hit content like "Toy Story 5."
Disney plans to increase cash content spending to $26 billion in fiscal 2027, up 9% from fiscal 2026, prioritizing international programming and sports rights.
Executives reiterated commitment to the "One Disney" model, integrating streaming and theme park operations to drive long-term margin expansion and shareholder growth.
title: Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts
